title: Jonah and the Ledger
premise: When a confession letter arrives at Vesper Coldharbour's office—postmarked the day after the funeral of the town's patriarch, Aldous Wren—the small-town coroner realizes the death he signed off as natural was anything but. The letter points to a ledger hidden in plain sight among the gravestones of Vesper Coldharbour itself, recording decades of payments, favors, and deaths that built the Wren family fortune on drowned secrets. As Vesper decodes it, he finds his own father's name in its columns and learns that staying invisible was never an option: the ledger was left to him deliberately, by someone who knew he'd have to read it. In the end, Vesper must choose between exposing the truth and letting the tide keep what it took—and he chooses to publish the ledger, burying the Wren dynasty but finally giving the dead their names back.
about_author: Orsen Blackwood is the pen name of a former maritime archivist who spent fifteen years cataloguing shipwreck records along the northern coast before turning to fiction. His novels are known for their tide-worn atmospheres and protagonists who speak more fluently to the dead than to the living.

chapters.title: The Weight of Names
chapters.summary: Vesper Coldharbour, coroner of a fading coastal town, prepares the body of Aldous Wren for burial, noting details about the corpse that don't quite match the official story. His POV establishes his intimacy with the dead and his deliberate invisibility among the living. Emotional beat: quiet unease beneath professional detachment.

chapters.title: Postmarked Yesterday
chapters.summary: A day after the funeral, a letter arrives confessing to Aldous Wren's murder—but unsigned, and postmarked from Vesper's own town. Vesper's POV; he reopens the file in secret. Emotional beat: the first crack in his safe, invisible life as duty collides with self-preservation.

chapters.title: What the Tide Keeps
chapters.summary: Vesper walks the shoreline where the letter suggests evidence lies, finding nothing but a stone marker with numbers scratched into it. Intercut with memories of his father, a fisherman lost at sea. Emotional beat: grief resurfacing, the sense that the past is not finished with him.

chapters.title: The Wren Estate
chapters.summary: Vesper pays condolences to the Wren family and observes the heirs: son Marcus, brittle widow Eleanora, and estranged granddaughter Ivy, who watches him too closely. Vesper's POV. Emotional beat: the realization that everyone in that house is performing grief—or hiding something worse.

chapters.title: Ledger in Plain Sight
chapters.summary: Vesper matches the stone-marker numbers to dates on gravestones in the old churchyard and discovers a pattern: every marked grave corresponds to a payment recorded nowhere. His POV, methodical decoding. Emotional beat: exhilaration curdling into dread as the scale becomes clear.

chapters.title: Ivy at the Door
chapters.summary: Ivy Wren appears at Vesper's office unannounced, asking pointed questions about her grandfather's autopsy. She reveals she found one page of a ledger years ago and never understood it. Alternating tension, mostly Vesper's POV. Emotional beat: wary alliance forming between two people who trust no one.

chapters.title: Entries 1974–1981
chapters.summary: Decoded entries reveal payments to town officials and a recurring notation: 'the sea settles accounts.' Several names match men officially lost at sea—including, Vesper realizes with horror, his own father. Vesper's POV. Emotional beat: devastation; the mystery has become personal.

chapters.title: The Sheriff's Silence
chapters.summary: Vesper cautiously probes Sheriff Dane Halloway, whose name appears in the ledger, and is met with a veiled threat dressed as friendliness. Vesper's POV. Emotional beat: fear—he understands now why the confessor stayed anonymous, and how dangerous visibility is.

chapters.title: Eleanora's Parlor
chapters.summary: Vesper visits the widow and finds her lucid in a way the town never credited; she quotes the ledger verbatim before pretending she said nothing. Her brief POV interlude hints she has been protecting someone for forty years. Emotional beat: pity tangled with suspicion.

chapters.title: The Second Letter
chapters.summary: Another letter arrives, this one naming a date three days hence and warning that 'the tide gives up what it took.' Vesper and Ivy compare notes and realize the writer knows both their histories intimately. Shared POV sections. Emotional beat: urgency—the confessor is running out of time or patience.

chapters.title: Marcus Wren's Debts
chapters.summary: Vesper digs into Marcus's finances and finds the estate nearly hollowed out, with Marcus desperate enough to sell the family's shipping company. Marcus's POV chapter shows him discovering his father's ledger references and panicking. Emotional beat: a suspect revealed as another victim of inheritance.

chapters.title: Grave Thirteen
chapters.summary: Following the ledger's oldest entry, Vesper opens a cold case: a girl drowned in 1968, ruled accidental, whose grave bears the thirteenth mark. He interviews the last living witness, now senile, who murmurs Aldous's name. Vesper's POV. Emotional beat: righteous anger hardening into resolve.

chapters.title: Someone Is Watching
chapters.summary: Vesper's office is searched; his copy of the decoded pages is gone. He suspects the sheriff but the intrusion feels amateurish, frightened. Vesper's POV, paranoid and sleepless. Emotional beat: isolation deepening—Ivy is the only person he can still trust, maybe.

chapters.title: The Confession's Handwriting
chapters.summary: Vesper compares the confession letters against old coroner files and recognizes the handwriting: it belongs to his predecessor, the late coroner Ruth Ellery, who died two years ago—which is impossible. Vesper's POV. Emotional beat: vertigo; the dead are writing to him.

chapters.title: Ruth's Boxes
chapters.summary: In Ruth Ellery's sealed storage, Vesper and Ivy find her complete investigation into the Wrens—and a draft confession she never sent, plus instructions addressed 'to whoever signs my cases next.' Vesper's POV. Emotional beat: awe and sorrow; Ruth chose him deliberately.

chapters.title: What My Father Carried
chapters.summary: The ledger's final column decodes: his father wasn't lost at sea—he was paid to sink a boat carrying a witness, then silenced himself. Vesper confronts the memory honestly for the first time. Vesper's POV. Emotional beat: the book's darkest hour; grief without anesthesia.

chapters.title: The Date Arrives
chapters.summary: On the promised day, the tide recedes unusually far, exposing the wreck of the witness's boat with remains and a locked strongbox aboard. Half the town gathers on the shore. Multiple POVs converge. Emotional beat: held breath—the past surfacing literally before everyone.

chapters.title: Strongbox
chapters.summary: Vesper claims jurisdiction over the remains and opens the strongbox privately: inside, documents proving Aldous ordered the drowning, and a second ledger page naming every accomplice—including the sheriff's father. Vesper's POV. Emotional beat: cold clarity; he holds the power corruption always wanted.

chapters.title: The Offer
chapters.summary: Sheriff Halloway offers Vesper a quiet burial for the evidence—money, protection, his father's name cleaned. Marcus, present and desperate, begs him to burn it. Vesper refuses. Climactic confrontation in the boathouse. Emotional beat: temptation met and turned away.

chapters.title: Storm Over Coldharbour
chapters.summary: Halloway moves to arrest Vesper on fabricated charges; Ivy releases Ruth's full file to the regional press as the storm knocks out the town's communications. Chaos, alliances shifting, Marcus turning state's evidence. Rapid multi-POV. Emotional beat: the climax—truth versus power, all cards down.

chapters.title: Every Grave by Name
chapters.summary: State investigators arrive; Halloway is taken, the Wren estate seized, and the drowned of forty years are formally identified. Vesper reads each name aloud at a public reckoning in the churchyard. Vesper's POV. Emotional beat: catharsis—the dead given back their names.

chapters.title: The Last Entry
chapters.summary: Months later, Vesper adds a final line to the ledger—his father's true story—and buries it at sea as the tide comes in. He accepts that visibility, like memory, is a cost worth paying. Final Vesper POV. Emotional beat: quiet peace; inheritance transformed into testimony.
